extracted.intended_audience: navigators, shipmasters, colonial administrators, engineers, and settlers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical navigational directions, tidal/seasonal guidance, and prescriptive recommendations for colonial infrastructure (railways, lighthouses) and convict employment/discipline drawn from a maritime/travel narrative. Contains procedural steps, site-selection criteria, and policy suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directions for entering Port Phillip (line-of-battle ship channel)
rubrics_metrics.description: After passing Point Nepean steer for Arthur's Seat, keeping Point Flinders open south of Lonsdale Point until the last cliffy projection is passed and bears South 1/4 West. Then steer half a point to the left of Arthur's Seat, shutting in Point Flinders with Point Nepean, and keeping Point Lonsdale a little open of the latter. The buoy at the eastern entrance should be kept in line with Arthur's Seat. Pass on the north side of the buoy and then haul up South-East until the water shoals to five fathoms, or until Whale Head bears South-West by West; then steer North-East by East for Mount Martha, the next hill north of Arthur's Seat, until the latter bears South-East, when a course may be shaped for Hobson's Bay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise procedural directions intended for large (line-of-battle) ships; the footnote expands on local bearings and visual marks (buoy alignment, bearings of hills/points) to be used when approaching the entrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tidal observations and implications for navigation at Port Phillip
rubrics_metrics.description: High-water at Shortland's Bluff on full/change: 12 hours 20 minutes. Simultaneous observations: William Town +1h0m; Under Arthur's Seat +1h45m; Corio Harbour +2h30m. Rise at springs at entrance only 3.5 feet; stream runs in at 2h0m; outward and inward streams differ (inward 5–5.5 hours; outward 6–7 hours). Outward stream between the heads may reach nearly 7 knots and, when opposed to a southerly gale, causes a dangerous sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local tidal timings and stream velocities to plan entry/exit; expect variation across the bay, stronger outward streams near the heads, and that southerly gales can heap water and mask tidal fall near the entrance. West Channel flood/ebb velocities 1–2.5 knots; little tidal stream above banks or in inlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directions for the western entrance of Bass Strait (passage guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The western entrance formed by islands off north-west Tasmania and Cape Otway is 108 miles wide; King Island lies near mid-channel occupying 35 miles. Passage between King Island and Cape Otway is safer than the southern passage (south of King Island) because the south passage is impeded by Reid's Rocks, Conway and Bell sunken rocks, Albatross Island and the Black Pyramid. The Harbinger Rocks and Navarin Rock constitute chief dangers in the safer entrance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masters should endeavour, if possible, to make land near Cape Otway; in thick weather, being in 60 fathoms of fine grey sand indicates you are in the fairway. Rocky bottom at that depth indicates a more southerly position (off west King Island). Be aware of doubtful reported sunken rocks and use soundings and landmarks to confirm position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighthouse siting criteria for Bass Strait
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer Cape Otway to Cape Wickham for a western-entrance lighthouse; for the eastern entrance, Kent Group (eastern island) is recommended as the best position for a light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a light on Cape Wickham might draw vessels dangerously near Harbinger Rocks and the western side of King Island if ships are south of their reckoning; a light on Cape Otway avoids bringing ships into that danger and, if a vessel is south of its position, the coast trend and soundings will reveal the error and allow safer passage. The Committee of the Legislative Council concurred with Cape Otway and Kent Group recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of depth and seabed composition to determine position in the Strait
rubrics_metrics.description: In the western entrance, sixty fathoms with fine grey sand indicates the fairway; in the same depth with a rocky bottom, a ship will be to the southward (off west King Island).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular lead soundings and noting sediment type (fine sand vs. rocky bottom) are practical means to ascertain whether a vessel is in the correct channel when visibility is poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal and barometric indicators for safe passage through Bass Strait
rubrics_metrics.description: January and February are the best months for a westward passage through Bass Strait. Prevailing gales begin at North-North-West and draw round by West to South-West. The barometer is a predictor: it is seldom fine when it registers less than 29.95, and bad weather is certain if it falls to 29.70.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan passages in the recommended months and monitor barometer and wind veering to avoid dangerous gales; understand typical gale progression and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigation advice for the south entrance of King Island
rubrics_metrics.description: If obliged to enter Bass Strait by the south entrance keep to the southward of Reid's Rocks, passing close to the Black Pyramid (dark rocky lump, 240 feet high) and make it bear North-East 3/4 East—this bearing keeps ships clear of the Conway and Bell sunken rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular attention must be paid to cross set of the tides and their sometimes-strong strength (up to 3 knots); timing of the south-west stream and its relation to high-water should be considered (stream to SW by S begins at 3 P.M. on full/change days, 3.5 hours before high-water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchorage selection and sheltering in the strait
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchorages in the strait should be sheltered from both east and west quarters because sudden shifts (easterly to westerly) occur; good holding-ground and an outset sweeping out of the bay lessen cable strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select anchorages with protection from both quarters; jetties may provide available shelter at high water for vessels of specified draught (example: a jetty sheltering vessels of nine to ten feet draught).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended railroad routing from Sydney (practical routing advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because country between Parramatta and Sydney is very hilly, perform that part by steamer; commence the railroad on the right bank about seven miles from the town. Extend the line into the north‑western interior; to the south pass round the head of Botany Bay and follow valleys trending southwards toward Illawarra to connect Manero corn country and the Illawarra coalfields with Sydney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Route choice aims to bring agricultural and coal resources into connection with Sydney to stimulate colony development and commerce; steamer use recommended where topography is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroad feasibility and benefits in Tasmania (north–south line)
rubrics_metrics.description: A railroad traversing Tasmania from north to south (Hobart–Launceston) would connect the Derwent with northern export points, draw export/import traffic to Hobart, stimulate trade and production, and restore prosperity; though a private company might not have immediate advantage, in a few years remunerative return could be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include cheaper and rapid intercourse, drawing export traffic to superior harbours, and long-term economic benefits; the suggestion to employ convict labour could reduce construction cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment of probationers/convicts on public infrastructure projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the population of probationers, pass-holders, and ticket-of-leave men (superabundant labour) to execute large public works (railroads, lighthouses). Capital could be supplied by a private company; convicts dispersed to islands could construct lighthouses, raise food nearby, and use local stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach would provide temporary relief to the labour market, lower construction costs, supply labour for needed works (reducing state expense), and could be made remunerative by levying light‑dues (example: about a penny a ton on passing vessels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles and reforms for convict discipline and rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The concentration of convicts in probation gangs is productive of harm: mixing the well-disposed with hardened offenders impedes reformation. The assignment system or dispersion (separating convicts among free settlers) better guards against 'evil communication' and aids moral improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended reforms include dispersing convicts rather than congregating them, providing separate sleeping cabins, granting occasional week-long holidays to whet desire for liberty, improving apparel in proportion to good conduct, and employing convicts in constructive work (railroads/lighthouses). These measures aim to promote rehabilitation and reduce moral corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tidal set and timing north of King Island (local tidal behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-water on full and change days at 1 o'clock; the stream begins to set to the South-West three hours and a half before high-water, running at 1–2 knots; past the Harbinger Rocks the set sweeps round to South-South-West sometimes at nearly 2.5 knots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these local timings and velocities when planning passage north of King Island; be mindful of where and when the stream changes direction and strengthens.
